In this VladTV interview, Rainwater details the Dallas tension involving comedian Roy Lee, Yella Beezy, and Mo3, explaining how internet jokes about Oak Cliff, North Dallas, and McKinney escalated into real-life violence. Rainwater says he introduced Roy Lee to Mo3 after seeing how artists and comedians like T.I. and Lil Duval connected, but claims Roy’s jokes about Yella Beezy led to him being jumped twice, including an incident at King of Diamonds involving Beezy’s circle and Joey Bodega.

Rainwater recalls Roy Lee being shot on September 25, 2018, saying Roy called him from the ambulance and later told him someone around Yella Beezy was responsible. He also describes visiting Roy with Mo3, Roy’s recovery at home, and the blood clot complications that led to his death on October 13, 2018. The conversation covers Dallas rap beef, street politics, and the aftermath of Roy Lee’s passing.

--------
In this VladTV interview, Jimmy DiModica recounts the years before his labor union involvement, describing a three-year run across the U.S. with what he calls a “precision” theft crew led by a master thief. DiModica details how distractions were used in regular stores—not just jewelry shops—from Kennebunkport, Maine, and Lake Geneva, Wisconsin, to Ocean City, Maryland, Detroit, Chicago, and Florida. He recalls one Circle K score where money was allegedly hidden in an old sneaker, and explains how the operation finally came under scrutiny after a Maryland pharmacy incident. DiModica also discusses being linked to the case through his father, the role of surveillance footage, the legal “Stet” outcome, and hiring the law office of Peter Angelos, former Baltimore Orioles owner. The conversation also touches on Milford Academy, the Baltimore Colts connection, and how this chapter led toward the union world.

Former La Eme made member Rene “Boxer” Enriquez sits down with VladTV to trace his path from Cerritos and Artesia 13 to San Quentin, Folsom State Prison and Pelican Bay. Enriquez discusses his family upbringing, early gang life, heroin addiction, prison politics, the Mexican Mafia’s “Black Hand,” and the violence that led to convictions in the Cynthia Galvan and David Gallegos murders.  

He also addresses the fallout around *American Me*, Edward James Olmos, Danny Trejo, Joe “Pegleg” Morgan, and the myths surrounding prison gang culture. After dropping out in 2002, Enriquez became a federal informant, testified in dozens of cases, and later fought parole reversals under California governors Jerry Brown and Gavin Newsom before his 2022 release.  

A rare firsthand account of crime, accountability, prison reform, and life after La Eme.

In this VladTV interview, John Franzese Jr. details the Nicky Bova situation and the moment he says mob associates discussed making him responsible for a planned hit—despite him never having killed anyone. Franzese explains how pressure from New York Mafia circles intensified while he was already cooperating with the FBI and secretly recording conversations, including around his father, a powerful underboss.  

The conversation covers alleged shakedowns tied to marijuana and cocaine dealers, references to cousin Michael, Tommy, a Gambino captain, California, New York, strip clubs, and the complicated Bova family connection. Franzese also reflects on addiction recovery, fear, loyalty, and why he stalled violent orders while gathering evidence for federal authorities.  

A rare firsthand look at Mafia cooperation, wiretaps, organized crime investigations, and the personal cost of turning against family.

--------
Former DEA agent Chris Feistl breaks down the tense hunt for Cali Cartel boss Miguel Rodríguez Orejuela in Colombia, revisiting details later dramatized in Netflix’s *Narcos* Season 3. Speaking with Vlad, Feistl explains how a delayed raid, missing paperwork, and an allegedly corrupt prosecutor allowed Miguel to avoid capture inside a hidden “caleta” compartment. He describes clues from informant Jorge Salcedo, including Panasonic phone systems, hypoglycemic food, and a secret desk compartment containing a ledger of 2,800 officials allegedly on the cartel payroll.

Feistl also recalls the danger facing Salcedo after the failed operation and how the DEA adjusted tactics for the August 1995 raid, securing approval for forced entry with a prosecutor brought from Bogotá. The result was a dramatic early-morning operation down a mountainside that led to Miguel’s capture, exposing the depth of Cali Cartel corruption and law enforcement risk.

In this VladTV full interview, Tito “TJ” Dominguez recounts his journey from a Cuban exile family in Havana to becoming a major 1980s cocaine transporter linked to Pablo Escobar and the Medellín Cartel. Dominguez details his early life in Miami and Haiti, the failed sugar mill project that pushed him into smuggling, and how marijuana runs through the Bahamas led to high-stakes cocaine flights from Colombia into Florida.

He discusses working near Escobar’s network, negotiating with cartel figures, encounters involving Carlos Lehder, George “Boston George” Jung, Manuel Noriega, and the realities behind *Blow*. Dominguez also opens up about his Lamborghini dealership, federal raids, CCE charges, money laundering case, solitary confinement, a failed helicopter escape plan, and life after prison with Miami Sun.

A firsthand account of crime, consequences, and survival during the cocaine era.

In this VladTV full interview, West Baltimore half-brothers Marlow Bates and Timmirror “Tamir” Stanfield share their account of the 1980s street era that helped inspire HBO’s Marlo Stanfield on The Wire. They discuss growing up in the projects, the rise of heroin in Baltimore, Murphy Homes, New York connections, and crossing paths with figures like Little Melvin Williams.

Bates and Stanfield also address their murder convictions, double-life sentences, claims of fabricated evidence, former detective Ed Burns, creator David Simon, and the impact of discredited ballistics expert Joseph Chaperro. The conversation covers Jamie Hector’s portrayal, prison life, losing family while locked up, and their release after nearly four decades.

Now focused on accountability and community, they reflect on the damage drugs caused in Baltimore, their Amazon Prime documentary People Say It’s Nice, and the TV project they say will tell more of their story.

Rainwater sits down with VladTV to reflect on his path from Dallas and Cedar Hill party promoter to managing Mo3 during the rapper’s rise. He opens up about serving time after burglary of habitation charges tied to college dorm break-ins, a jail experience that changed his outlook, and how he met Mo3 shortly after coming home in 2014. Rainwater recalls hearing Mo3’s music through a woman named Crystal, comparing his voice to “the next Kurt Cobain,” then building a close business relationship based on a 50/50 handshake deal with no paperwork. The interview also looks at the DFW rap scene, Oak Cliff, early booking work with dance-era artists, and the long-running tension between Mo3 and Yella Beezy, who Rainwater says were often around each other but never truly close.
